# Practice and solutions

::: {.chapter-lead}
Try each question before opening its solution. These are classroom exercises, not a graded or secure test. The website does not submit your answers to a teacher.
:::

## 1 · Draw from a frequency table

Thirty students recorded school-shuttle waiting times. Use **5-minute bins from 0 to 30** and the left-inclusive, right-exclusive rule. Draw a histogram on paper with labelled axes, equal-width touching bars, and a zero baseline.

| Waiting time (minutes) | Frequency |
|:--|--:|
| $0\leq x<5$ | 3 |
| $5\leq x<10$ | 7 |
| $10\leq x<15$ | 10 |
| $15\leq x<20$ | 6 |
| $20\leq x<25$ | 3 |
| $25\leq x<30$ | 1 |

After drawing, use the digital check to reconstruct your heights. It checks heights only, not the labels on your paper.

<div class="interactive" data-widget="draw-check"><p>Enter six bar heights, check them against the table, and view your attempt.</p></div>

<details class="solution"><summary>Show the completed histogram</summary>

<div data-chart="shuttle" class="chart-frame"></div>

Heights are **3, 7, 10, 6, 3, 1**, totaling 30. Every bar is 5 minutes wide. The tallest bar means ten waits from 10 to under 15 minutes—not ten waits exactly equal to 10.

</details>

## 2 · Stem, leaf, and key

Construct a stem-and-leaf plot for **1.2, 1.5, 1.5, 2.0, 2.3 seconds**. Explain the repeated leaf.

<details class="solution"><summary>Show solution</summary>

```text
1 | 2 5 5
2 | 0 3
Key: 1 | 2 = 1.2 seconds
```

Five leaves represent five observations. The repeated 1.5 needs two leaves of 5. A zero leaf preserves the 2.0-second observation.

</details>

## 3 · Bin boundaries

Which 10-minute commute bin contains 20? Does the first occupied bin prove the recorded minimum is 0?

<details class="solution"><summary>Show solution</summary>

20 enters **$20\leq x<30$**, not the preceding bin. The first occupied bin establishes a value in **$0\leq x<10$**, not necessarily 0. The original list—not the histogram—identifies the minimum as 5.

</details>

## 4 · Repair turnaround times

Describe the histogram of **40 bicycle repairs**. Find the percentage taking at least 4 hours. Can you recover the most common exact time?

<div data-chart="repairs" class="chart-frame"><p>One-hour bins from 0 to 8: frequencies 12, 10, 7, 5, 3, 2, 1, 0.</p></div>

<details class="solution"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Repair times are **unimodal and right-skewed**, centered around **1–3 hours**. Values occupy bins from 0 to under 7 hours. No displayed internal bin is empty. The one observation in 6–7 hours is not automatically an outlier; an empty final 7–8 bin is not an internal gap.

At least 4 hours: $(3+2+1)/40=15\%$. The most frequent **interval** is 0–1 hour. The most common exact value is not recoverable.

</details>

## 5 · Two concentrations

Describe shape, center, spread, and the empty internal interval for these **40 library study sessions**. What percentage lasted from 30 to under 90 minutes?

<div data-chart="sessions" class="chart-frame"><p>Fifteen-minute bins from 0 to 120: frequencies 2, 10, 8, 0, 0, 8, 10, 2.</p></div>

<details class="solution"><summary>Show solution</summary>

The displayed distribution is **approximately symmetric and bimodal**, with main concentrations in **15–45 and 75–105 minutes**. The visual center near **60 minutes** lies in a gap, not at a typical observed session. Occupied bins span roughly **0–120 minutes**. There are no observations from **45 to under 75 minutes**.

The count from 30 to under 90 is $8+0+0+8=16$, giving $16/40=40\%$. A single center would hide the two concentrations. The exact median is not available from the histogram.

</details>

## 6 · What could be inside a bin?

Two commute times lie in 40–50 and one in 50–60 minutes. How many are at least 40? How many could be at least 45?

<details class="solution"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**Exactly 3** are at least 40. **Between 1 and 3** could be at least 45: the last-bin observation definitely qualifies; either, neither, or both observations in the preceding bin might qualify. Do not add a uniformity assumption.

</details>

## 7 · Oxygen: count and context

Return to the [oxygen histogram](worked-examples.qmd#oxygen-example). How many sampled cold streams recorded below 6 mg/L? What percentage is this? What does the empty 3–4 bin establish?

<details class="solution"><summary>Show solution</summary>

The first four counts total $1+0+1+1=3$. The percentage is $3/429\times100\%\approx0.7\%$. Under our convention, no observed concentration lies in $3\leq x<4$ mg/L. This does not show that such concentrations are impossible in all streams.

</details>

## 8 · Repair a weak description

A student writes, “The graph is high in the middle and goes up and down.” Replace this with all four parts of a contextual description.

<div data-chart="review-dot" class="chart-frame"><p>Twenty review-session lengths span 4–30 minutes, with approximate symmetry and a broad central concentration.</p></div>

<details class="solution"><summary>Show a model response</summary>

Among these 20 students, review-session lengths are **approximately symmetric with one broad central concentration**, centered around **16–18 minutes**. Recorded values extend from **4 to 30 minutes**, with no clearly isolated observation or large internal gap.

The dotplot preserves individual values, so the observed endpoints are available. Wide histogram bins would warrant less exact wording.

</details>

## Before the next class

Explain **one dot versus one bin**, construct a histogram from a table, name skew from the tail, and support a claim with **calculation + context**. Return to the relevant chapter when an answer depends on a guess rather than evidence.
